title: Gut Motility, Secretion and Gut Hormones

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In healthy humans, half of a glass of water leaves the stomach in about 10 minutes, but half of a high-calorie liquid may remain after about 2 hours. Why?
cards.back: Calories reaching the duodenum release hormones and start nerve reflexes that slow the stomach. Water carries no calories, so it meets no calorie brake.
cards.why: The slowing goes beyond what the drink's thickness alone would do.
cards.quote: When calories reach the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, it releases hormones and starts nerve reflexes that slow the stomach.

cards.front: Name three ways the vagus acts on the gut before food arrives (the anticipation exception to on-then-brake control).
cards.back: The cephalic phase of acid secretion, relaxation of the stomach as you swallow, and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
cards.quote: The vagus can act on a part before food arrives: the cephalic phase of acid secretion, the stomach's relaxation as you swallow, and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.

cards.front: What is a slow wave in gut smooth muscle, and is it an action potential?
cards.back: A rhythmic depolarization lasting seconds, about 3 per minute in the human antrum. It is not an action potential; it sets when the muscle can contract.
cards.quote: These are slow waves: rhythmic depolarizations lasting seconds, about 3 per minute here.
cards.section: Reading a slow-wave recording

cards.front: In a recording from human antral smooth muscle, why are some slow waves followed by a contraction and others not?
cards.back: A contraction follows only when a wave carries the muscle past threshold for Ca2+ entry, the voltage at which its Ca2+ channels open. Those waves have a higher plateau, sometimes with spikes.
cards.quote: A contraction follows only when a wave carries the muscle past threshold for Ca2+ entry, the voltage at which its Ca2+ channels open.
cards.section: Reading a slow-wave recording

cards.front: In humans, slow waves run about 3 per minute in the antrum, about {{c1::11 to 12}} per minute in the duodenum and about 8 to 9 per minute in the ileum.
cards.quote: about 11 to 12 per minute in the duodenum and about 8 to 9 in the ileum
cards.section: Reading a slow-wave recording

cards.front: In the metronome-and-pianist picture of gut motility, what do slow waves set, and what do neurons and hormones set?
cards.back: Slow waves (the metronome) set the beat: when a contraction can happen. Neurons and hormones (the pianist) set whether each wave carries the muscle past threshold, and how far: the coupling to contraction.
cards.why: Force generation itself belongs to the smooth muscle.
cards.quote: Slow waves are a metronome, fixing the beat.
cards.section: The metronome and the pianist

cards.front: Excitatory enteric neurons are driven maximally in human duodenal muscle. About how many phasic contractions per minute can the muscle make at most, and why not more?
cards.back: About 11 to 12 per minute, the local slow-wave rate. Stronger input makes more waves reach threshold and raises force, but each phasic contraction needs a slow wave.
cards.why: The slow-wave rate is the ceiling on phasic contraction rate in the small intestine and antrum.
cards.quote: the slow-wave rate is the fastest rate at which a region can repeat a phasic contraction
cards.section: The metronome and the pianist

cards.front: Which cells generate the slow waves of gut smooth muscle?
cards.back: Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC): branched cells that form networks between and within the muscle layers. Isolated ICC show the rhythm; isolated smooth muscle cells typically do not.
cards.quote: it comes from the interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC), branched cells that form networks between and within the muscle layers
cards.section: Where the beat comes from

cards.front: In paired recordings from mouse gut muscle, slow waves were larger in myenteric ICC than in the smooth muscle beside them. What does this show about how the muscle gets its slow waves?
cards.back: The waves start in ICC and reach the muscle passively, shrinking as they spread; the muscle does not regenerate them.
cards.quote: slow waves were larger in myenteric ICC than in the smooth muscle beside them
cards.section: Where the beat comes from

cards.front: W/Wv mice carry Kit mutations and have few myenteric ICC, but their smooth muscle and enteric neurons are present. Predict their small-intestinal slow waves, and state what the result shows.
cards.back: Slow waves are absent (a second laboratory found the same). ICC are necessary for the rhythm; neurons cannot stand in for the missing clock.
cards.why: Neurons are the pianist, not the metronome: they adjust coupling but do not make the waves.
cards.quote: W/Wv mice, with mutations in Kit, a receptor ICC need to develop, have few myenteric ICC.
cards.section: Where the beat comes from

cards.front: Kit-mutant mice lack myenteric ICC and slow waves. Neonatal mice lacking the Ca2+-activated Cl- channel ANO1 (TMEM16A) have normal-looking ICC networks but no slow waves. What does the second result add?
cards.back: ANO1 is needed to run the clock, separately from building it. In the proposed model, periodic Ca2+ release in ICC opens ANO1, giving the depolarizing current of the slow wave.
cards.why: The knockout data come from neonatal mice, not adults or a human disorder.
cards.quote: Mice born without it had normal-looking ICC networks, yet their gut muscle failed to develop slow waves
cards.section: The channel in the film

cards.front: Name the two plexuses of the enteric nervous system and the main job of each.
cards.back: Myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus: mainly movement. Submucosal (Meissner's) plexus: mainly secretion and local blood flow.
cards.quote: the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus mainly for movement and the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus mainly for secretion and local blood flow
cards.section: The gut wall has its own nervous system

cards.front: In peristalsis (the law of the intestine), what does a local stimulus such as a distending bolus produce on each side of it?
cards.back: Contraction on the oral side and relaxation on the anal side, so contents are driven anally.
cards.quote: produced contraction on the oral side and relaxation on the anal side, so contents were driven anally
cards.section: The gut wall has its own nervous system

cards.front: In loops of dog small intestine, the extrinsic nerves (vagi and splanchnics) were cut and peristalsis was tested. What happened, and what does it show?
cards.back: Peristalsis survived; it was lost only when nervous conduction within the wall was blocked. Nerves in the gut wall carry the reflex without the central nervous system.
cards.why: The experiment did not show which neurons or transmitters carry it.
cards.quote: The reflex survived, and was lost only when nervous conduction within the wall was blocked
cards.section: The gut wall has its own nervous system

cards.front: Contrast the internal and external anal sphincters: muscle type and control.
cards.back: Internal: smooth muscle, not under voluntary control, relaxed by an enteric reflex when the rectum distends. External: skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve, with resting contraction and voluntary squeeze.
cards.quote: The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve
cards.section: The gut wall has its own nervous system

cards.front: In a test preparation, nerve conduction within the rectal wall is blocked while all extrinsic nerves are intact. A balloon in the rectum is inflated. Predict the internal anal sphincter's response, and why.
cards.back: It fails to relax. Relaxation of the internal sphincter on rectal distension is an intrinsic enteric reflex, carried by nerves in the wall.
cards.quote: When it is distended, an enteric reflex relaxes the internal anal sphincter, which is smooth muscle and not under voluntary control.
cards.section: The gut wall has its own nervous system

cards.front: Human salivary flow rises sharply. Predict the tonicity of the saliva compared with saliva at low flow, and explain from the two-step model.
cards.back: Closer to plasma tonicity. Acinar fluid starts near plasma; the water-poorly-permeable ducts then reabsorb Na+ and Cl-. At high flow they have less time per volume, so less salt is removed.
cards.quote: At high flow the ducts have less time per volume and the saliva comes out closer to plasma tonicity.
cards.section: Mouth to stomach: wet, swallow, store, grind, meter

cards.front: Distinguish receptive relaxation from accommodation in the upper stomach.
cards.back: Receptive relaxation: on swallowing, the vagus relaxes the upper stomach before food arrives. Accommodation: distension keeps it relaxed through vagal and local reflexes. Either way volume rises with little pressure rise.
cards.quote: When you swallow, the vagus relaxes the upper stomach before the food gets there (receptive relaxation), the anticipation exception at work.
cards.section: Mouth to stomach: wet, swallow, store, grind, meter

cards.front: How does the human antrum grind food?
cards.back: Contractions timed by slow waves push chyme against a closing pylorus; most chyme is thrown back, until particles are small enough to pass.
cards.quote: push chyme, the soupy mix of food and juice, against a pylorus that is closing, and most of the chyme is thrown back
cards.section: Mouth to stomach: wet, swallow, store, grind, meter

cards.front: Which hormones released by nutrients in the small intestine slow gastric emptying, and through what route in part?
cards.back: CCK (duodenum) and, further down, GLP-1. Partly through vagal reflexes that slow the antrum and tighten the pylorus.
cards.quote: Nutrients reaching the duodenum release CCK and, further down, GLP-1, and these slow emptying
cards.section: Why the milkshake waits: the duodenal brake

cards.front: A human stomach hands on calories at a steady 2 kcal per minute. How long does it take to deliver half of a 600 kcal liquid meal to the duodenum?
cards.back: Half is 300 kcal; 300 / 2 kcal per min = 150 min, about 2.5 h.
cards.why: The duodenal brake meters calories at roughly 1 to 4 kcal per minute, so caloric liquids tend to empty at a more nearly steady rate.
cards.quote: The stomach hands calories on at roughly 1 to 4 kcal per minute.
cards.section: Why the milkshake waits: the duodenal brake

cards.front: Water leaves the human stomach roughly losing half of what remains every 10 minutes. What fraction of a drink of water remains after 30 minutes?
cards.back: Three halvings: 0.5 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.125, about 12.5 percent.
cards.quote: roughly losing half of what remains every 10 minutes
cards.section: Why the milkshake waits: the duodenal brake

cards.front: Describe the three phases of the migrating motor complex in the fasting gut.
cards.back: Phase I (about 45 to 60 min): slow waves but few or no contractions. Phase II: irregular contractions. Phase III: a 5 to 15 minute front of strong contractions sweeping toward the pylorus and down the small bowel.
cards.quote: Phase III is a 5 to 15 minute front of strong contractions that sweeps toward the pylorus and down the small bowel.
cards.section: Between meals: the migrating motor complex

cards.front: What controls when MMC phase III starts in the human antrum, and which hormones can trigger it?
cards.back: Enteric neurons, with vagal and hormonal input, decide when the front starts and how it moves. Plasma motilin rises in cycles, and intravenous motilin or ghrelin can start antral phase III.
cards.quote: plasma motilin rises in cycles, and in humans intravenous motilin or ghrelin can start antral phase III
cards.section: Between meals: the migrating motor complex

cards.front: Where is the parietal cell's H,K-ATPase at rest, and where does stimulation put it?
cards.back: At rest in cytoplasmic tubulovesicles; stimulation moves it into the membrane of the secretory canaliculus, a deep fold of the apical surface.
cards.quote: Stimulation moves the pumps into the membrane of the secretory canaliculus, a deep fold of the apical surface.
cards.section: Acid from a pump, protection from a gel

cards.front: The gastric H,K-ATPase exchanges H+ for K+ electroneutrally. How, then, does HCl accumulate in the lumen?
cards.back: K+ returns to the lumen through apical channels and Cl- exits with it, so H+ and Cl- both build up while K+ recycles.
cards.quote: K+ returns to the lumen through apical channels and Cl- exits with it, so HCl accumulates
cards.section: Acid from a pump, protection from a gel

cards.front: Where does the parietal cell's secreted H+ come from, and what is the alkaline tide?
cards.back: Carbonic anhydrase makes the H+. The matching HCO3- leaves across the basolateral membrane in exchange for Cl-, adding base to the blood: the alkaline tide.
cards.quote: the matching HCO3- leaves across the basolateral membrane in exchange for Cl-, the alkaline tide of acid-base balance
cards.section: Acid from a pump, protection from a gel

cards.front: Give the receptor, G protein and second messenger for each of the parietal cell's three acid switches.
cards.back: Acetylcholine: M3, Gq, Ca2+. Gastrin: CCK2, Gq, Ca2+. Histamine: H2, Gs, cAMP.
cards.quote: histamine acts on Gs-coupled H2 receptors and raises cAMP
cards.section: Acid from a pump, protection from a gel

cards.front: Fasted human volunteers were given gastrin. Blocking H2 receptors abolished the acid response, and muscarinic block sharply cut the response to the lower dose. What do the two results imply?
cards.back: In humans gastrin probably acts mainly by releasing histamine from ECL cells beside the parietal cells, and acetylcholine is a needed partner.
cards.quote: muscarinic block cut the response to the lower dose sharply, so acetylcholine is a needed partner
cards.section: Acid from a pump, protection from a gel

cards.front: In the cephalic phase of gastric acid secretion, by what two routes do vagal signals raise acid?
cards.back: Vagal fibres excite enteric neurons: some release acetylcholine onto parietal cells; others release gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), which makes antral G cells release gastrin.
cards.quote: others release gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), which makes G cells in the antrum release gastrin
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: Which cells release gastrin, and what stimulates them in the gastric phase?
cards.back: G cells in the antrum. Stimuli: digested peptides and amino acids acting directly (for example via the calcium-sensing receptor), vagal input through GRP neurons, and distension reflexes.
cards.quote: Digested peptides and amino acids act on G cells directly, sensed through receptors such as the calcium-sensing receptor.
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: How does acid in the antrum limit its own production?
cards.back: Acid makes antral D cells release somatostatin, which holds back the neighbouring G cells: negative feedback, the more acid, the less gastrin.
cards.quote: acid makes D cells release somatostatin, and somatostatin holds back the G cells beside them
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: A patient takes a proton pump inhibitor daily for months. Predict plasma gastrin, and what happens when the drug is stopped.
cards.back: Gastrin rises: little acid reaches the antrum, D cells release less somatostatin, and G cells are released from restraint. On stopping, the extra drive shows up as rebound acid.
cards.quote: Little acid reaches the antrum, so D cells release less somatostatin, and the G cells, no longer held back, release more gastrin.
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: In the intestinal phase, which duodenal hormones inhibit gastric acid, which cells make them, and what releases each?
cards.back: Secretin from S cells, released by acid; CCK from I cells, released by fat and digested protein. CCK also slows emptying, so the intestinal phase is mostly a brake.
cards.quote: Acid entering the duodenum releases secretin from S cells, and fat and digested protein release CCK from I cells.
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: Why does the stomach not digest its own surface?
cards.back: A mucus gel traps the bicarbonate that surface cells secrete against the lining, so the surface is far less acidic than the lumen. Prostaglandins sustain mucus and bicarbonate; tight junctions limit H+ back-leak.
cards.quote: A layer of mucus gel traps the bicarbonate that surface cells secrete and holds it against the lining
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: A drug sharply reduces prostaglandin production in the gastric mucosa. Predict the effect on the mucosal surface.
cards.back: Less mucus and bicarbonate, so the surface is less shielded from luminal acid and more open to injury.
cards.why: Prostaglandins keep the mucus and bicarbonate barrier coming.
cards.quote: Prostaglandins keep that mucus and bicarbonate coming, and tight junctions between the cells limit how much H+ leaks back in
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: Estimate the minimum free energy to move 1 mol H+ from parietal cytosol (pH 7.0) to a lumen at pH 1.0 at 310 K, assuming electroneutral exchange (R = 8.314 J/mol/K). Can one ATP (about 55 kJ/mol) move two H+?
cards.back: delta-G = 2.303RT x delta-pH = 5,936 J/mol per pH unit x 6 = about 35.6 kJ per mol H+. Two H+ would cost 71.2 kJ, more than 55 kJ, so only one H+ per ATP.
cards.why: Ignoring the uphill K+ step makes this a minimum.
cards.quote: Two H+ at pH 1 would cost 71.2 kJ, too much.
cards.section: Worked problem: what does it cost to make pH 1?

cards.front: With cytosolic pH 7.0, 2.303RT = 5.94 kJ/mol per pH unit and 55 kJ per ATP, could the gastric pump afford 2 H+ per ATP at a luminal pH of 3.0? What is the lowest luminal pH at which 2 per ATP stays affordable?
cards.back: At pH 3.0: 2 x 5.94 x 4 = 47.5 kJ, under 55, so affordable. Limit: delta-pH at most 55 / (2 x 5.94) = 4.6, a luminal pH of about 2.4.
cards.why: Whether the pump actually moves 2 H+ per ATP at milder pH is debated; the budget only sets what is affordable.
cards.quote: Two per ATP stays affordable while 2 x 5.94 x delta-pH is at most 55, so delta-pH is at most 4.6
cards.section: Worked problem: what does it cost to make pH 1?

cards.front: Mice lacking the CCK-B (gastrin) receptor: predict basal gastric pH and plasma gastrin compared with wild type, and give the mechanism.
cards.back: pH higher (3.2 to 5.2) and gastrin about 10-fold higher. Gastrin cannot drive acid, so less acid reaches the antrum, less somatostatin restrains G cells, and gastrin rises.
cards.why: The same lost acid brake as with a proton pump inhibitor.
cards.quote: basal gastric pH rose from 3.2 to 5.2, and plasma gastrin was about 10-fold higher
cards.section: Cutting a switch, or losing the brake

cards.front: A gastrinoma releases gastrin that acid cannot suppress. Predict plasma gastrin, acid output and gastric pH, and explain why stools may turn fatty.
cards.back: Gastrin stays high, basal acid output and parietal cell mass rise, and gastric pH falls. Duodenal pH falls low enough to inactivate pancreatic lipase, so fat leaves undigested.
cards.quote: Duodenal pH falls low enough to inactivate pancreatic lipase, the enzyme that digests fat, so fat leaves undigested.
cards.section: Cutting a switch, or losing the brake

cards.front: Two patients both have high plasma gastrin. One has high gastric pH; the other has very low gastric pH. Interpret each.
cards.back: High gastrin with high pH: lost acid feedback (for example proton pump inhibitor use, atrophic gastritis). High gastrin with low pH: an autonomous source that ignores the brake, such as a gastrinoma.
cards.why: Reading gastrin and acid together separates the two; diagnosis still needs further tests.
cards.quote: Gastrin is high in both cases while acid moves in opposite directions, so reading the two together points to lost feedback or to an autonomous source
cards.section: Cutting a switch, or losing the brake

cards.front: Compare a histamine H2 blocker with a proton pump inhibitor in a human: predict plasma gastrin under each, and why the extra gastrin fails to restore acid in either case.
cards.back: Gastrin rises under the proton pump inhibitor (less acid, less antral somatostatin), and an H2 blocker is expected to do the same if it cuts acid. Gastrin's probable main human route, ECL histamine, is blocked by the H2 blocker; under the proton pump inhibitor the pump downstream is blocked.
cards.why: Rests on the D-cell feedback loop and on gastrin acting mainly via ECL histamine in humans.
cards.quote: The extra gastrin cannot bring the acid back to normal, because the block sits downstream, at the pump
cards.section: Switching acid on and off

cards.front: What does secretin drive in the human pancreas, and how concentrated is the product?
cards.back: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, reaching 140 to 150 mM HCO3-, about 6- to 7-fold over plasma, by a CFTR-dependent route.
cards.quote: in humans the juice reaches 140 to 150 mM HCO3- under secretin, about 6- to 7-fold over plasma
cards.section: The duodenum answers back

cards.front: A person lacks working CFTR in pancreatic duct cells. Predict duodenal pH after an acidic meal and a likely consequence for fat digestion, from the lesson's rules.
cards.back: Secretin cannot drive the CFTR-dependent bicarbonate secretion, so duodenal acid is poorly neutralized and pH stays lower. Low duodenal pH can inactivate pancreatic lipase, so fat digestion may suffer.
cards.why: Combines the CFTR-dependent duct route with the gastrinoma rule that low duodenal pH inactivates lipase.
cards.quote: by a route that depends on CFTR
cards.section: The duodenum answers back

cards.front: Give the cell, stimulus and main actions of CCK in the duodenum.
cards.back: I cells; fatty acids and digested protein. Contracts the gallbladder, drives acinar enzyme secretion, slows gastric emptying, and inhibits acid (CCK1 receptors).
cards.quote: CCK and acetylcholine drive acinar enzyme secretion, CCK contracts the gallbladder
cards.section: The duodenum answers back

cards.front: In a patient, a high-calorie liquid meal empties as fast as water. Which control system is most likely failing, and where would you look?
cards.back: The duodenal calorie brake: nutrient release of CCK and GLP-1, or the vagal reflexes that slow the antrum and tighten the pylorus.
cards.why: Without the brake, a caloric liquid meets no more resistance than water.
cards.quote: these slow emptying, partly through vagal reflexes that slow the antrum and tighten the pylorus
cards.section: Why the milkshake waits: the duodenal brake

cards.front: A biopsy in diabetic gastroparesis shows few antral ICC but normal-looking enteric neurons. Predict the antral electrical recording, and whether solids or liquids empty worse.
cards.back: Slow waves absent, small or irregular, so contractions are sparse and poorly timed. Solids suffer most, because antral grinding needs the clock; liquids depend more on upper-stomach tone and are often spared.
cards.why: A biopsy shows association, not cause.
cards.quote: Solids should suffer most, because antral grinding needs the clock.
cards.section: Design problem: a stomach that cannot grind

cards.front: Gastrin-deficient mice have no basal acid, and even histamine, which acts directly on parietal H2 receptors, cannot induce acid; days of gastrin partly restore it. Explain, and name one test.
cards.back: Gastrin is trophic as well as acute: without it the acid-secreting unit is not built or maintained, leaving little for histamine to act on. Test: count parietal cells and measure H,K-ATPase and H2 receptor against wild-type littermates.
cards.quote: Propose that gastrin is trophic as well as acute
cards.section: Design problem: a stomach without gastrin

cards.front: Isolated mouse small intestine makes migrating complexes without slow waves. Can this show that human antral MMC phase III does not need slow waves, or test motilin's role?
cards.back: No. It has not been shown for the human stomach, where phase III contractions ride on slow waves, and mice make no working motilin, so they cannot test the motilin side.
cards.quote: Isolated mouse small intestine can make migrating complexes without slow waves, which has not been shown for the human stomach.
cards.section: Between meals: the migrating motor complex
